title: 2 Kings 25:13–21
context: The Chaldeans break up the bronze pillars, stands, and sea and carry off the temple vessels, and the narrator recalls the size of the pillars Solomon made. Nebuzaradan takes the chief priests, officials, and sixty men of the land to Riblah, where the king of Babylon has them put to death, and Judah is carried away captive out of its land. Both traditions read this as shared ground, and the capital height in 25:17 and the number of the king’s advisers in 25:19 differ from Jeremiah 52:22 and 52:25.

verses.text: The Chaldeans broke up the pillars of bronze that were in the LORD’s house and the bases and the bronze sea that were in the LORD’s house, and carried the bronze pieces to Babylon.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The Chaldeans broke up the pillars of bronze that were in the LORD’s house and the bases and the bronze sea.” Arminian readers note the dismantling of the temple furnishings Solomon had made (1 Kings 7:15–39).

The bronze is carried to Babylon.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the loss of the pillars, named Jachin and Boaz (1 Kings 7:21), as a sign of the end of an era.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the temple’s visible glory is removed under judgment.

verses.text: They took away the pots, the shovels, the snuffers, the spoons, and all the vessels of bronze with which they ministered.
verses.arminianNotes:
“They took away the pots, the shovels, the snuffers, the spoons, and all the vessels of bronze with which they ministered.” Arminian readers note that the tools of temple worship are taken away.

The list records the loss in ordinary detail.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the end of the sacrificial service as it had been practiced in Jerusalem.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the vessels later reappear in the account of the return (Ezra 1:7–11).

verses.text: The captain of the guard took away the fire pans, the basins, that which was of gold, for gold, and that which was of silver, for silver.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The captain of the guard took away the fire pans, the basins, that which was of gold, for gold, and that which was of silver, for silver.” Arminian readers note the thoroughness of the plunder.

The wording stresses the value of the metals.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the temple’s wealth taken as Isaiah had warned (20:17).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the riches that once marked Solomon’s temple are carried away.

verses.text: The two pillars, the one sea, and the bases, which Solomon had made for the LORD’s house, the bronze of all these vessels was not weighed.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The two pillars, the one sea, and the bases, which Solomon had made for the LORD’s house, the bronze of all these vessels was not weighed.” Arminian readers note the great quantity of bronze.

The phrase recalls 1 Kings 7:47.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the narrator linking the loss directly to Solomon’s work.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the end of the temple is set against the memory of its building.

verses.text: The height of the one pillar was eighteen cubits, and a capital of bronze was on it. The height of the capital was three cubits, with network and pomegranates on the capital around it, all of bronze; and the second pillar with its network was like these.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The height of the one pillar was eighteen cubits... The height of the capital was three cubits.” Arminian readers note that 1 Kings 7:16 and Jeremiah 52:22 give five cubits for the capital.

The difference is noted without resolution.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note the difference in the height of the capital and leave it unresolved.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the description recalls the craftsmanship now lost.

verses.text: The captain of the guard took Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the second priest, and the three keepers of the threshold;
verses.arminianNotes:
“The captain of the guard took Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the second priest, and the three keepers of the threshold.” Arminian readers note that the temple’s leaders are taken.

Ezra 7:1 names a Seraiah in Ezra’s ancestry.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the priesthood brought under judgment along with the king.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the leaders of worship share the fate of the city.

verses.text: and out of the city he took an officer who was set over the men of war; and five men of those who saw the king’s face, who were found in the city; and the scribe, the captain of the army, who mustered the people of the land, and sixty men of the people of the land who were found in the city.
verses.arminianNotes:
He takes an officer over the men of war, “five men of those who saw the king’s face,” the scribe, and sixty men of the land. Arminian readers note that Jeremiah 52:25 says seven men.

The difference is noted without resolution.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note the number difference with Jeremiah 52:25.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the officials and leaders of the city are taken to Riblah.

verses.text: Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard took them, and brought them to the king of Babylon to Riblah.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard took them, and brought them to the king of Babylon to Riblah.” Arminian readers note that Riblah is where Zedekiah was also judged (25:6).

The narrative moves to the final judgment on the leaders.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the leaders brought before the conqueror.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground, read soberly: those responsible for the city’s resistance face Babylon’s judgment.

verses.text: The king of Babylon attacked them and put them to death at Riblah in the land of Hamath. So Judah was carried away captive out of his land.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The king of Babylon attacked them and put them to death at Riblah in the land of Hamath. So Judah was carried away captive out of his land.” Arminian readers note the plain report of the executions.

The final sentence fulfills the warnings of Deuteronomy 28:36.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the exile completed as the LORD had warned.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground and read it soberly: Judah’s removal from the land is the climax of the book’s account of judgment.
